question: What is the primary goal of infection control in the obstetric theatre?

options.A: To speed up the turnover time between surgical procedures
options.B: To break the chain of infection by eliminating pathogens
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of hospital-acquired drugs
options.D: To ensure compliance with hospital administrative audits

explanation: Infection control focuses on stopping harmful germs from reaching the mother or baby during surgery. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h1)

question: Who holds responsibility for maintaining safety in the obstetric operating theatre?

options.A: The sterile supply department technicians alone
options.B: The hospital infection control manager exclusively
options.C: Only the consultant obstetrician on duty
options.D: Every member of the surgical team

explanation: Theatre safety requires active vigilance and participation from all healthcare staff present in the room. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h1)

question: How does aseptic technique differ from general medical asepsis?

options.A: It allows the presence of non-pathogenic bacteria on instruments
options.B: It strives for an environment free of all pathogens and spores
options.C: It is only used outside the operating room environment
options.D: It focuses exclusively on handwashing with plain soap and water

explanation: Aseptic technique aims for total absence of living microorganisms, whereas medical asepsis only reduces their numbers. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h2)

question: When must a midwife strictly apply aseptic techniques in obstetric care?

options.A: Only when cleaning the general walls of the labour ward
options.B: During procedures like caesarean sections and catheterizations
options.C: During daily ward rounds when talking to stable patients
options.D: Whenever performing routine antenatal abdominal palpation

explanation: Invasive procedures that breach natural body barriers require strict asepsis to prevent infection. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h2)

question: Which processing method destroys all microbial life including bacterial spores?
explanation: Sterilization is the only process among the three that guarantees the total destruction of resistant spores. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of the initial decontamination step for surgical instruments?

options.A: To remove organic matter and blood so subsequent steps work effectively
options.B: To achieve complete sterilization before the instruments are autoclaved
options.C: To dry out moisture and prevent corrosion of metal joints
options.D: To replace chemical disinfectants with plain tap water rinsing

explanation: Cleaning away blood and tissue debris prevents organic matter from shielding microorganisms during sterilization. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h3)

question: What is the standard physical method used for steam sterilization in hospitals?

options.A: Autoclaving using moist heat under pressure
options.B: Dry heat baking in a standard kitchen oven
options.C: Boiling instruments in open water for ten minutes
options.D: Ultraviolet radiation exposure in a closed box

explanation: Autoclaves use pressurized steam to effectively kill all forms of microbial life on medical equipment. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h4)

question: How can a midwife quickly check if a wrapped instrument tray has been through an autoclave cycle?

options.A: By looking at the colour change on the external chemical indicator tape
options.B: By checking the weight of the metal container on a weighing scale
options.C: By smelling the interior wrapping paper for a distinct chemical scent
options.D: By feeling the temperature of the metallic package with bare hands

explanation: Chemical indicator tape changes colour when exposed to the proper sterilization heat parameters. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h4)

question: In what direction should a midwife scrub their arms during a surgical scrub?

options.A: From the fingertips down toward the elbows
options.B: In a random circular motion over the hands
options.C: Starting directly at the middle of the forearm
options.D: From the elbows down toward the fingertips

explanation: Scrubbing from the cleanest area (fingertips) to the less clean area (elbows) prevents dirty water from flowing back onto the hands. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h5)

question: Why must hands remain elevated above the elbows after a surgical scrub?

options.A: To prevent water and contaminants from flowing downward from the arms
options.B: To make it easier for the circulating nurse to tie the back gown strings
options.C: To allow the surgical gown to slip on much faster without friction
options.D: To keep the skin cool and reduce sweating inside the sterile gloves

explanation: Gravity would pull contaminated rinse water from the forearms back down onto the surgically clean fingers if hands were lowered. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h5)

question: How should a midwife react to a sterile drape that has become wet during an operation?

options.A: Cover the wet spot with an extra layer of dry sterile gauze
options.B: Leave it alone since moisture has no effect on sterile boundaries
options.C: Dry the wet area quickly with a clean unsterile theatre towel
options.D: Treat it as contaminated because moisture permits bacterial strike-through

explanation: Wet drapes allow liquids and bacteria to pass through from underneath, breaking the sterile barrier. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h6)

question: What is the correct movement protocol when working around an established sterile field?

options.A: Reach across the sterile table whenever you need an extra instrument
options.B: Always face the field and never turn your back on it
options.C: Walk quickly around the room with your back turned to save time
options.D: Keep your arms lowered below your waistline at all times

explanation: Turning your back on a sterile field risks accidental contamination from unsterile parts of your gown. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common source of contamination in the operating theatre?

options.A: Air currents stirred up by excessive staff movement
options.B: Unsterile items touching the edges of a sterile table
options.C: Punctured surgical gloves unnoticed by the wearer
options.D: Using sterile instruments well within their expiry date

explanation: Properly sterilized instruments kept within date are safe and do not cause contamination. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h7)

question: What should a midwife do immediately upon noticing a colleague break sterile technique?

options.A: Document the error in the nursing notes without telling the surgeon
options.B: Wait until the operation finishes and report the incident in private
options.C: Ignore the mistake if the senior doctor was the one who made it
options.D: Speak up immediately to correct the breach and protect the patient

explanation: Patient safety comes first, and breaches must be addressed immediately to prevent surgical site infections. [learn more](BMP116_U5_T2#BMP116_U5_T2_h7)
